title: Pacing practice and building endurance
summary: Practise five minutes, rest five, to avoid muscle spasm; endurance matters.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: The only thing I can say about blowing the cornet is practice, when you practice, practice for five minutes and then lay the horn down for five minutes. So that you build up your em bou chure (muscles?) rather than overdo it and get a charlie horse you know.
Oh, you can get a muscle spasm?
Well you get a muscle spasm up here in your lips.

You know if you overblow your lip will swell up on you. So that what you need most of all is practice for endurance. And if you try to blow it too much at one time without warming up, you're liable to get a charlie horse up there and that's no good. In other words, you must warm up. The more practice you do the better, but space it. Time it. Practice for five, ten minutes as you go. I mean if you're starting, just beginning, just practice you know five minutes that's all. And then rest for five minutes or so and then come back again and play. And that way you build up, you build up your muscles for endurance is what you build them up for. Same as an athlete. He can't go out without, be out of condition and go out and play a football game or a baseball game. If you're not in condition you're not going to make it. You're going to get a charlie horse.
And you do have to play for hours. (LAUGHTER).
We have to play for hours.
And especially when you go into these jam sessions as you used to that lasted all night long. (LAUGHTER).
Well that's the way we do it. you know. You're playing all the time anyway.
That's fun yes, but it's still you know, you're body has to go on, yes.
That's what I'm saying, you need it. Yes.

And then that way when you have good endurance and you're blowing correctly your lips get better and better instead of tightening up on you. Gosh with the old Pollack band years ago, boy, we used to record in the day time and then go and play in the Park Central at night and when we finished there we'd go on to Harlem and jam you know.
